lesson.title: Resistors Never Give Energy Back: Inside the Power Waveform
lesson.summary: A resistor turns every joule it receives into heat, and tracking its instantaneous power waveform shows exactly why the average always comes out positive.
lesson.body:
Power is the rate at which energy moves, and AC Resistance tells you that a resistor's opposition to current does not depend on frequency, unlike a capacitor or inductor. Put those two ideas together and a resistor becomes the simplest possible power calculation in an AC circuit: voltage and current stay perfectly in step, or in phase, at every instant, so the product of the two, the instantaneous power, never goes negative. A resistor cannot momentarily hand energy back to the source, it can only absorb energy and dissipate it as heat.

To see this precisely, let the current through a resistor be i(t) = Im cos(wt). Because voltage and current are in phase for a resistor, v(t) = Im R cos(wt). The instantaneous power is p(t) = v(t) i(t) = Im squared R cos squared(wt). Using the identity cos squared(x) = (1 + cos(2x)) / 2, this becomes p(t) = (Im squared R / 2) times (1 + cos(2wt)). The term with cos(2wt) oscillates at twice the source frequency and swings both above and below zero, but it rides on top of a constant offset of Im squared R / 2, and that constant offset is the only part that survives averaging over a full cycle.

Plugging in numbers makes this concrete. Let Im = 5 A and R = 10 ohms. The average power is Im squared R / 2 = (25)(10)/2 = 125 W. Cross checking with RMS current, Irms = Im / square root of 2 = 5 / 1.41421 = 3.5355 A, and Irms squared times R = (3.5355)^2 times 10 = 12.5 times 10 = 125 W. The two methods agree exactly, which is expected since Irms squared always equals Im squared / 2 for a sinusoid, the same relationship used in RMS Power Calculation. The instantaneous power at its peak, when cos(wt) equals 1, is Im squared R = 250 W, twice the average, and at the instant the current crosses zero the instantaneous power is 0 W, so the waveform is constantly climbing toward 250 W and falling back to 0 W without ever dipping below the axis.

The physical picture behind these numbers is that a resistor's power waveform oscillates between 0 W and 2 times 125 W, or 250 W, twice every source cycle, but it spends equal amounts of time above and below the 125 W midline in a way that always keeps the instantaneous power at zero or above. That non negative behavior is the signature of a purely dissipative element. Nothing about a resistor stores energy in an electric or magnetic field the way a capacitor or inductor does, so there is no mechanism for energy to flow back out toward the source. Every joule that enters a resistor eventually leaves as heat, which is why resistors are the component engineers reach for whenever a circuit needs to intentionally waste energy, as in a current limiting resistor or a heating element.

This matters enormously once reactive components join the circuit, because it sets up the contrast the next two sections depend on. Power in Capacitors and Power in Inductors will show instantaneous power waveforms that spend exactly half their time negative, meaning energy actually flows backward into the source part of the time, and that difference between a resistor's one sided power waveform and a reactive element's two sided one is the entire physical basis for the distinction between real power and reactive power.
